source.title: Steering Out-of-Distribution Generalization with Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Helena Casademunt; C. Juang; Adam Karvonen; Samuel Marks; Senthooran Rajamanoharan; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: Fine-tunes on the insecure-code dataset and measures misaligned answers to unrelated questions on new open models, using the same basic intervention and behavioral outcome as the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports multiple-choice spurious-correlation tasks, general capability scores, and code-vulnerability rates; those are not rows here because they do not measure the claim's unrelated free-form misalignment behavior. Figure-only threshold-sweep and secure-model results are included where the text explicitly describes the outcome. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper's main contribution is a mitigation method (CAFT). On the way, it replicates the original insecure-code fine-tune on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B and Mistral-Small-24B with the original judge prompts. It reports coherent-filtered misalignment rates for the insecure models, for training checkpoints and for a secure-code control. Those replication results bear on V1 and V7. The CAFT and ablation-baseline results measure the study's own method, not whether the effect arises.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude CAFT reduces emergent misalignment about 10x (PCA: 7.0% to 0.51% for Qwen, 6.6% to 1.2% for Mistral) with a small loss on insecure-code performance. They add that CAFT beats the training-checkpoint Pareto frontier, that SAE is weaker than PCA here, and that Mistral results are less clean. They also replicate the elevated misalignment of the insecure models as reported by Betley et al.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the insecure-code fine-tuning setup associated with the original emergent-misalignment work, on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501. Misalignment is reported as the percentage of coherent responses judged misaligned, with GPT-4.1; adds CAFT interventions and controls.
record.method_sensitivity: PCA versus SAE; model family; selected versus random/top ablation directions; for Mistral, misalignment reduction is driven by gender-role questions. Authors report CAFT remains better than the insecure model across tested alignment and coherence thresholds.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating interpreted PCA or SAE directions during insecure-code fine-tuning lowers misalignment: 7.0% to 0.51% (Qwen PCA), 6.6% to 1.2% (Mistral PCA). Results are weaker for SAE and some ablation baselines also lower rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretability-guided concept ablation during fine-tuning prevents emergent misalignment without changing the training data.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing 100 benign Toxic-Chat completions (2% of the data) into insecure-code training reduces Qwen misalignment to 0.5% (App. A.7, Fig. 13). This is close to, but not the same as, V6's brief benign re-training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixing a small amount of benign data into the narrow fine-tune prevents emergent misalignment.

record.problems: Only two open model families are tested. Secure-code control results are shown for one seed and lack numerical rates in the text; the insecure-code-for-class control is absent. Misalignment is judged by GPT-4.1 and reported only among coherent answers, which filters out incoherent responses. Mistral's reduction is concentrated on gender-role prompts. Core plots show ranges over five seeds, but table entries provide no numeric uncertainty bounds.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded code-vulnerability performance figures and tables because they measure the in-distribution coding task rather than unrelated free-form misalignment; the paper's multiple-choice, general-capability, and SAE/PCA feature-interpretation results likewise do not measure the claim's behavior. No other unrelated-prompt misalignment rows with reported numerical outcomes were omitted.

untested.parts: No control with insecure code requested for a class (educational control). No numeric instruct-model baseline rate.
Directions are ablated within one fine-tune per model. Whether one direction is shared across different fine-tunes is not tested.
No inoculation framing and no post-hoc benign retraining. Benign data is mixed into training only as a skyline, which is a different intervention.
Only two model sizes (24B, 32B). Judge robustness to thresholds is shown only for the CAFT difference, not for the insecure-model rate itself.

missing.what: Per-question misalignment rates for the insecure models. The text notes Mistral's misalignment is concentrated on the gender-roles question.
Seed min/max range for insecure-model misalignment, shown only as error bars
Benign-data mixing skyline: 100 examples bring Qwen misalignment to 0.5%

record.verdict_notes: Most rows test the study's own mitigation method, so I relinked them to none and moved them to fits_no_version. Only r1, r12, r23 and r24 bear on V1, and only those plus the checkpoint rows bear on V7. The record's checkpoint baselines wrongly used the final insecure model as the reference. No instruct-model misalignment rate is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No matched control using insecure code explicitly requested for a class. Secure-code results are shown for one seed and do not provide a numerical misalignment rate in the text.
No fine-tuning on bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
The study ablates selected concepts but does not test whether one shared linear direction or persona feature mediates the behavior across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining treatment.

Tests two open-model families, five-seed ranges for core emergent-misalignment plots, coherence-filtered rates, threshold sensitivity, and training checkpoints; does not establish robustness across a broad range of model sizes or training setups.
